### The Things We Keep Until Friday

On Fridays, the city sent a truck for everything nobody had come back for. The driver was named Len. He wore a clean shirt to do dirty work and never asked why a thing had been saved. At four, he backed up to the municipal lost-property office and waited for Ruth to open the loading door.

The office occupied the old weights-and-measures building, which meant that people sometimes came in wanting to know if their grocer was cheating them. Ruth always wished she could help. It would have been satisfying to put an onion on a scale and settle something.

Instead, she had umbrellas.

She had a clarinet with a note in the case that said, in a child’s handwriting, *Please do not make me play this at Grandma’s*. She had a single roller skate, size eleven, with four immaculate wheels. She had six copies of a book called *Getting Your Life in Order*, five of them left on buses and one found in the courthouse, where it had apparently been used to prop open a window.

And, beginning on a Tuesday in October, she had a kitchen drawer.

A street sweeper had found it on a traffic island. The drawer was pine, painted yellow, with a brass handle that had gone green around the screws. It contained two birthday candles, a screwdriver, red thread, a packet of soy sauce, and a key with a cardboard tag marked *NOT THIS ONE*.

Ruth put it on the shelf behind her desk. Several people asked about it, but nobody claimed it. A man collecting a briefcase reached in for the screwdriver without asking. Ruth held out her hand until he gave it back.

At lunch she ate an apple over the drawer, careful not to drop any seeds inside. She tried to remember what had been in the kitchen drawer of the apartment where she grew up. Batteries, probably. Her father’s reading glasses. A little wrench that came with something they no longer owned. For years after he died, she had been able to recall the sound of him searching that drawer. Now when she tried, what she heard was herself asking him what he was looking for.

About three weeks after the drawer came in, a woman in a blue raincoat stopped at the counter.

“Is that from a kitchen?” she asked.

“I assume so,” Ruth said.

“We had those handles.”

“Do you want to look at it?”

The woman said no, then took off her gloves. Ruth set the drawer on the counter.

The woman picked up the key. “My son used to write things like this. We had a switch in the hall that didn’t do anything, and he put a piece of tape over it that said ‘Don’t.’ I asked him why, and he said, ‘Because it doesn’t.’”

“How old is he?”

“Thirty-one. He works at an aquarium. I don’t know what he does there, exactly. He tells me and I come away with the impression he fixes the fish.”

She put the key back and collected the gloves she’d come for. They were black wool, joined at the wrists by a long cord.

“People laugh,” she said, threading the cord through her sleeves, “but I still have them.”

On the drawer’s last Friday, Len came in early. Rain was coming under the loading door, and he helped Ruth move a box of books out of its path. Then he went to get a broom.

“Do you want a drawer?” she asked when he came back.

“What for?”

She hadn’t prepared for this question. “It’s a good drawer,” she said.

Len turned it over. On the underside someone had written *14⅜* in pencil.

“It’ll be that wide at the back,” he said. “Maybe a little wider at the front.”

He took a tape measure from his pocket. It was a little wider at the front.

“Made it to fit,” he said, and set it down.

At ten to four a man came in carrying a new umbrella with the price tag still on it. He had lost an old umbrella. Ruth showed him the stand by the radiator, and he sorted through it, opening two of them despite the sign.

“It had a wooden handle,” he said. “My wife bought it for me on our honeymoon. We’d had a fight, and I walked out in the rain. She came and found me in a sandwich shop. She’d bought herself one, too. Hers was better.”

He tried the last umbrella. It stuck halfway open.

“She’s at home,” he said, though Ruth hadn’t asked. “She told me to buy a new one.”

He folded the old umbrella and put it back. Then he asked Ruth for scissors so he could cut the tag off the new one before he went out.

By four the rain had eased. Len took the books and the umbrellas, the roller skate and the clarinet. Ruth carried the drawer as far as the loading door. She stood there holding it while Len tightened a strap across the back of the truck.

“I could take it home,” she said.

Len tested the strap with his thumb. “Sure.”

She thought of her kitchen. The shallow cupboard beside the stove had a shelf at just the right height, though she’d have to move the colander. She could put the scissors in there, and the loose batteries from the windowsill. She could throw out the soy sauce.

Instead she put the drawer on the truck.

On Monday morning there was a message from a man whose kitchen cabinets had fallen off a trailer in October. Ruth called him back. He said he wasn’t after cabinets, which were easy enough to replace. He wanted a brass handle. They’d found eleven in the road and needed twelve.

She told him about the truck. He was quiet a moment, then asked whether she remembered what the handle looked like.

She drew it while he waited: two square feet, a low arch, a screw at either end. He said there was a man at the flea market who sold handles out of coffee cans. He hadn’t been sure what to ask for.

Ruth offered to mail him the drawing. After they hung up, she went over the pencil lines in ink so they wouldn’t rub off in the envelope.
